 Finding grace in the storm 
 ‘Forest Gump’ actor Gary Sinise recalls his son’s courageous battle with cancer 
 By wpeditor 
 on 
 November 07, 2026 
 By Michele Willer-Allred 
 michele@theacorn.com 
 McCanna “Mac” and Gary Sinise Courtesy photos 
 The storm that tested Lt. Dan in “Forrest Gump” was nothing compared with the one Gary Sinise and his family faced when his son was diagnosed with a rare cancer.
 But during a Nov. 1 appearance at the Reagan Library, the actor, who portrayed the wounded Vietnam veteran Lt. Dan Taylor in the 1994 film, said it was his son, McCanna “Mac” Sinise, who taught him how to face life’s hardest moments with courage, grace and faith.
 The 71-year-old Sinise spoke with retired Reagan Library Director John Heubusch about his new book, “Graceful Warrior: The True Story of a Son, a Father, and a Family Who Carried Each Other Through.” The memoir is scheduled for release Nov. 10, Mac’s birthday.
 Sinise’s acting credits also include “Apollo 13,” “The Green Mile” and “CSI: NY.” He also founded the Gary Sinise Foundation in 2011 to support veterans, first responders and their families, and he performs for military audiences with the Lt. Dan Band.
 POWER OF TWO—Mac Sinese, a musician and composer and the son of actor Gary Sinese, was diagnosed at 27 with chordoma, a rare form of bone cancer. He didn’t survive. Gary Sinese wrote an inspirational account of the family’s struggle in a book called “Graceful Warrior,” which he discussed with the public in a Nov. 1 appearance at Reagan Library. 
 His previous memoir, “Grateful American: A Journey from Self to Service,” was co-written with Marcus Brotherton, who also helped write “Graceful Warrior.”
 Mac, a musician and composer, was diagnosed at 27 with chordoma, a rare form of bone cancer. He was the only son in the family of three children Sinise shares with his wife, Moira. Mac died in January 2024 after years of treatment. He was 33.
 Sinise connected his son’s experience to a pivotal “Forrest Gump” scene in which Lt. Dan struggles with guilt and shame during a hurricane.
 “He’s wrestling with God at that moment, that storm is raging inside of him . . . and he wins,” Sinise said.
 Sinise saw his son fighting his own storm. Mac became paralyzed from the chest down, and tumors spread throughout his body. Still, he continued making music. In early 2023, he returned to a piece he had written in college and asked his father to help finish recording it with his band.
 “It floored me. It’s such a beautiful piece,” Sinise said. 
 Mac recorded more music with the help of friends and taught himself to play the harmonica from his hospital bed. His work became the three-album “Resurrection and Revival” series, with proceeds benefiting the Gary Sinise Foundation.
 “He was screaming back with strength, courage, bravery and faith,” Sinise said.
 The family faced other serious challenges. Moira was diagnosed with Stage 3 breast cancer in 2018, which is now in remission. Sinise’s parents suffered strokes and became disabled, requiring the family’s care.
 “It just felt like the storm was raging around us all the time,” Sinise said.
 Still, Mac found ways to appreciate each day, even as the cancer spread.
 “He continued the fight but had such grace in the way he handled it and shaped his days,” Sinise said. “It was beautiful to witness it. My son, to me, is someone I just admire so much.”
 Mac found a silver lining in the way the illness helped bring him closer to his family. Sinise recalls his wife telling him Mac had said that, without the disease, he might have been traveling and pursuing his music career. Instead, he had time to talk with his mother, watch Cubs games, and be with family.
 “That’s a blessing,” Mac told her.
 Sinise also recalled taking a road trip with Mac when his son was 26, before the diagnosis. Despite work and touring commitments, he was grateful they had shared the time together.
 “I just thank God I didn’t put it off,” he said, describing the trip as precious and important. He urged parents not to wait for special occasions to spend time with their children, even after they become adults.
 “You got to make time with your family members,” he said.
